title: 1 Samuel 4:12–22
context: A Benjaminite runs from the battle to Shiloh with the news; the city cries out, and when Eli, ninety-eight and blind, hears that his sons are dead and the ark captured, he falls backward and dies after judging Israel forty years. His daughter-in-law, hearing the news, gives birth and, dying, names the child Ichabod, saying the glory has departed from Israel because the ark was taken. Both traditions read these deaths soberly as shared ground: the fulfillment of God’s word against Eli’s house and grief over the loss of God’s presence.

verses.text: A man of Benjamin ran out of the army and came to Shiloh the same day, with his clothes torn and with dirt on his head.
verses.arminianNotes:
A man of Benjamin runs from the army to Shiloh the same day, his clothes torn and dirt on his head. Arminian readers note the customary signs of mourning that announce disaster before he speaks.

The narrative slows to follow the news to Eli.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the messenger’s appearance as a silent announcement of catastrophe (cf. 2 Sam 1:2).

The speed of his arrival, “the same day,” heightens the sense that judgment has come swiftly.

verses.text: When he came, behold, Eli was sitting on his seat by the road watching, for his heart trembled for God’s ark. When the man came into the city and told about it, all the city cried out.
verses.arminianNotes:
Eli sits by the road watching, “for his heart trembled for God’s ark.” Arminian readers note that Eli’s deepest concern is for the ark, which shows real, if belated, devotion.

The whole city cries out when the man arrives.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see Eli’s fear for God’s ark as a sympathetic portrait of him in the narrative.

The narrator holds together Eli’s failure toward his sons and his genuine reverence for God’s presence.

verses.text: When Eli heard the noise of the crying, he said, “What does the noise of this tumult mean?” The man hurried, and came and told Eli.
verses.arminianNotes:
Eli hears the outcry and asks, “What does the noise of this tumult mean?” Arminian readers note the suspense as the blind old man must rely on sound.

The messenger hurries to tell him directly.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the tension building toward the climax of judgment.

Eli’s question echoes the Philistines’ question in verse 6, as both sides react to noise they cannot yet interpret.

verses.text: Now Eli was ninety-eight years old. His eyes were set, so that he could not see.
verses.arminianNotes:
Eli is ninety-eight years old, and his eyes are set so that he cannot see. Arminian readers note his frailty and dependence on others.

The detail explains why he waits by the road and why he must ask what the noise means.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the old priest’s weakness emphasized just before his fall.

The note recalls 3:2 and prepares the reader for his sudden death in verse 18.

verses.text: The man said to Eli, “I am he who came out of the army, and I fled today out of the army.” He said, “How did the matter go, my son?”
verses.arminianNotes:
The man says he has fled from the army, and Eli asks, “How did the matter go, my son?” Arminian readers note Eli’s gentle address, the same he used for Samuel (3:6, 16).

The short dialogue delays the blow.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the suspense held for a moment before the full report.

Eli’s tender question shows a father’s and priest’s fear for what has happened.

verses.text: He who brought the news answered, “Israel has fled before the Philistines, and there has been also a great slaughter among the people. Your two sons also, Hophni and Phinehas, are dead, and God’s ark has been captured.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The messenger reports flight, great slaughter, the deaths of Hophni and Phinehas, and the capture of God’s ark. Arminian readers note the escalating order, ending with the ark.

Each item is heavier than the last.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the climax: “God’s ark has been captured.”

The report fulfills what God told Samuel and the man of God before him (2:34; 3:11–14).

verses.text: When he made mention of God’s ark, Eli fell from off his seat backward by the side of the gate; and his neck broke, and he died, for he was an old man and heavy. He had judged Israel forty years.
verses.arminianNotes:
When the ark is mentioned, Eli falls backward from his seat, breaks his neck, and dies; he had judged Israel forty years. Arminian readers note that it was news of the ark, not of his sons, that broke him.

His death is told soberly and with some pity.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the judgment on Eli’s house falling on Eli himself.

The mention of his forty years as judge honors his long service even as it marks its end. Both traditions read the scene with sobriety rather than triumph.

verses.text: His daughter-in-law, Phinehas’ wife, was with child, near to giving birth. When she heard the news that God’s ark was taken and that her father-in-law and her husband were dead, she bowed herself and gave birth; for her pains came on her.
verses.arminianNotes:
Phinehas’ wife, near to giving birth, hears that the ark is taken and her father-in-law and husband are dead, and she goes into labor. Arminian readers note the shock bringing on her pains.

The tragedy now reaches the next generation of Eli’s house.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the far-reaching effects of judgment on a priestly house.

The narrator lists her griefs in the order she hears them, beginning with the ark.

verses.text: About the time of her death the women who stood by her said to her, “Don’t be afraid, for you have given birth to a son.” But she didn’t answer, neither did she regard it.
verses.arminianNotes:
As she is dying, the women tell her not to be afraid because she has borne a son, but she does not answer. Arminian readers note that her grief overwhelms even the comfort of a son’s birth.

The moment is told with restraint and great sadness.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see despair at the loss of God’s presence that no earthly comfort can reach.

The birth of an heir to the priestly line brings no consolation in the face of the ark’s capture.

verses.text: She named the child Ichabod, saying, “The glory has departed from Israel!” because God’s ark was taken, and because of her father-in-law and her husband.
verses.arminianNotes:
She names the child Ichabod, saying, “The glory has departed from Israel!” Arminian readers note that Ichabod means “no glory.”

The name expresses grief over the ark, her father-in-law, and her husband.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the loss of God’s visible glory from Israel (cf. Ps 78:61; Ezek 10:18 for a later departure of glory).

The child’s name becomes a lasting memorial of judgment on Eli’s house.

verses.text: She said, “The glory has departed from Israel; for God’s ark has been taken.”
verses.arminianNotes:
She repeats, “The glory has departed from Israel; for God’s ark has been taken.” Arminian readers note that the second statement focuses only on the ark.

The chapter ends in grief and loss.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the climactic lament of the chapter.

Yet the next chapter shows that God’s glory was not defeated by the Philistines; it was Israel that lost the ark through its own unfaithfulness.
